title: External Sorting & Aggregation
short: Sorting when the data exceeds RAM
lead: Count the reads and writes required when sorting or aggregation must process more data than fits in RAM.
goals: Connect query execution to the implementation of individual operators
Calculate the number of passes in two-way and multiway external merge sort
Compare reading through clustered and unclustered B+ trees

sections.title: From ORDER BY to external merge sort
sections.html:
Sorting supports ORDER BY, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, merge joins, and bulk loading. With a multi-column key, lexicographic order compares the first column first and considers each later column only when the preceding columns are equal. When the data exceeds RAM, it must be divided into smaller pieces and read and written sequentially. Relying on virtual memory alone does not make an in-memory algorithm efficient.

Follow values as well as runs

A merge compares the current heads of sorted runs. For [1,4,4] and [2,4,7], take 1 and advance the first input; take 2 and advance the second. The remaining heads are both 4. Taking and advancing each matching head retains all three copies, followed by 7, giving [1,2,4,4,4,7]. DISTINCT keeps one representative from each adjacent equal-key group, producing [1,2,4,7]; grouped aggregation instead combines that group’s values while scanning. Sorting preserves copies until an explicit elimination or aggregation step.

New worked example: sort 90 pages using 6 buffer frames allocated to the algorithm. Each frame holds one page.

  1. Pass 0: read 6 pages into RAM, sort them, and write a run, which is a sorted sequence. Repeat until all the data has been processed, producing 90/6=15 runs.
  2. Reserve 5 frames for reading 5 runs and 1 frame for collecting output. Repeatedly take the smallest item among the 5 inputs, append it to the output, and advance that input. One merge pass combines the 15 runs into 3 runs.
  3. The next merge pass combines the 3 runs into 1. The run counts are therefore 15→3→1, requiring 3 passes in total, including pass 0.

Every pass reads 90 pages and writes 90 pages, giving 2×90×3=540 page I/Os. This count includes writing the final result to disk and excludes CPU cost.

The general pass formula in the next section assumes N>0 input pages, B≥3 buffer frames, and materialised output, meaning the result is written to disk. An empty input requires no data-page sorting I/O. A nonempty input that fits in RAM costs one read and one final write, or 2N I/Os, under this convention. Pipelining can omit the final write. DISTINCT and aggregation can shrink output or use state unlike the input pages; do not reuse a sort formula that writes every original page on every pass without checking operator semantics.

sections.title: Count the passes and avoid unnecessary sorting
sections.html:
Let N be the number of pages to sort and B the number of buffer frames. Pass 0 processes up to B pages at a time, producing ceil(N/B) runs. Here ceil means rounding up, because a partial final batch still needs a run. Each merge pass combines at most B−1 runs because 1 frame must be reserved for output.

Repeat the merging until only 1 run remains. For N>0 and B≥3, the total number of passes is 1+ceil(log_(B−1)(ceil(N/B))). The initial 1 counts pass 0; the logarithm counts the merges in groups of B−1, rounded up. If each pass reads and writes all the data, the cost is 2×N×the number of passes. For two-way merge sort that creates one-page runs and merges 2 runs at a time, the pass count is 1+ceil(log2 N).

Key takeaway

Count the runs and passes before substituting into a formula. Pipelining the final output directly into the next operator may avoid the final write, but state that assumption before subtracting any I/O.

A B+ tree provides key order. With a clustered index, records with nearby keys are also close together in the data file, making leaf-order access attractive. With an unclustered index, fetching complete records in index order may require one random fetch per tuple. Tuples and pages are different units.

Related source material: PDF pages 12–17. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

sections.title: GROUP BY retains state, not necessarily every tuple
sections.html:
Original worked example: sales(region,amount) contains (North,10), (South,8), and (North,14). To calculate AVG, keep a hash-table entry containing sum and row count for each region. Reading (North,10) creates North→(10,1); (South,8) creates South→(8,1); (North,14) finds North’s entry and updates it to (sum=24,count=2). Divide at output: North gives 24/2=12 and South gives 8/1=8. MIN, MAX, SUM, and COUNT also have running state, so they need not retain every tuple.

Key takeaway

To combine averages, keep both the sum and the count. When two groups have different row counts, averaging their two averages does not give the combined average.

Size the aggregation state and account for skew

Memory is limited by this state, not necessarily by the input’s raw row count. A million copies of one key can collapse to one DISTINCT entry or a small SUM/COUNT state. Many distinct groups grow the hash table instead. If it no longer fits in RAM, partition input onto disk by group key, then build the running state for one partition at a time using a hash function independent of the partitioning function. With B buffer frames, partitioning reserves 1 input frame and B−1 output frames for B−1 partitions.

In a simple capacity model, if each partition subsequently fits into about B pages of RAM, the two phases can process approximately B(B−1) pages. This is only an estimate: overhead and skew may reduce the practical capacity, while combining state early may reduce the data that must be retained.

The simple B(B−1) capacity estimate assumes B−1 approximately equal spill partitions and about B pages for one partition’s hash table. If overhead factor f expands N/(B−1) data pages into fN/(B−1) state pages, that state must fit the memory actually allocated. For N=90, B=10, and f=1.2, each average partition needs 1.2×90/9=12 pages of state, exceeding 10. The average bound also cannot guarantee success when one partition is much larger than the rest.

Recursive repartitioning can separate distinct keys in an oversized partition, but cannot separate identical group keys. Their state must be combined or handled specially rather than repeatedly applying another hash function. The fit check must use state pages, hash-table overhead, and the actual memory allocation, as the calculation above illustrates.

Related source material: PDF pages 19–32. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

sections.title: Exercise: sorting or hashing?
sections.html:
Suppose a query needs DISTINCT customer_id without any ordering. The requirement then changes to DISTINCT customer_id ORDER BY customer_id. How does that affect your choice?

Show the solution

Hashing is a candidate for the first query because it only needs to eliminate duplicate keys. The second query requires order, so sorting can both bring duplicate keys together for elimination and produce the required output order. Costs still need to be compared; no choice is best for every dataset.

Repeat the calculation with 90 pages and 10 buffer frames. Pass 0 produces 90/10=9 runs. Reserving 1 output frame leaves 9 input frames, so all 9 runs can be merged in one merge pass. There are 2 passes in total, costing 2×90×2=360 I/Os if the final output is also written.

Related source material: PDF pages 18–32. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

quiz.question: For N=90 and B=6, how many I/Os does multiway sorting require when the final output is written?
quiz.explanation: The run sequence 15→3→1 requires 3 passes, each costing 180 I/Os.
